chapters.title: The Demo Is a Liar
chapters.tease: A demo proves something can happen. Production needs to know how often, and what the fifth case looks like.

chapters.title: Model, Tools, Loop
chapters.tease: An agent is a model, a set of tools and a loop. You rent the model; you own the tools and the loop.

chapters.title: The Loop Has a Body
chapters.tease: The model proposes and the harness disposes: every check between request and action is code you control.

chapters.title: Autonomy Is a Dial
chapters.tease: Autonomy is not something a system has or lacks. It is a dial you set per action, per risk and per stage.

chapters.title: When Not to Build an Agent
chapters.tease: The most valuable architectural decision is often the one that removes the agent entirely.

chapters.title: Defining Done
chapters.tease: A run ends when the harness verifies done, or in a clean, labelled failure, never on the model's say-so.

chapters.title: Nondeterminism Is the Weather
chapters.tease: The same input can take many paths. Make every path safe, and measure rates instead of anecdotes.

chapters.title: The Harness Is the Product
chapters.tease: Agent quality is mostly harness quality: context, tools, validation, limits and checks around the model.

chapters.title: Monday Morning Is a Test
chapters.tease: Monday morning meets the world at its least forgiving. If your agent survives it, it will survive the week.

chapters.title: Reliability Is an Engineering Job
chapters.tease: Prompting shapes what an agent tends to do. Engineering decides what it can do, and how you find out.

chapters.title: Start With One Agent
chapters.tease: One agent with good tools and a clear task beats a team of agents nine times in ten. Earn the org chart.

chapters.title: Workflows Versus Agents
chapters.tease: In a workflow, code decides the path. In an agent, the model does. Nest a bounded agent in a workflow spine.

chapters.title: Prompt Chaining
chapters.tease: Break a task into fixed steps, each a focused model call, and put cheap, specific checks between them.

chapters.title: Routing
chapters.tease: Classify each request first, then send it down a route built for its kind. Cheap, and it compounds.

chapters.title: Parallelisation and Voting
chapters.tease: Sectioning splits independent work to save time. Voting repeats work to turn randomness into confidence.

chapters.title: Orchestrator and Workers
chapters.tease: A lead agent splits an open task at run time, briefs fresh workers and synthesises what they return.

chapters.title: Evaluator and Optimiser
chapters.tease: One call drafts, a fresh evaluator critiques against a concrete rubric, and the rounds are capped.

chapters.title: Subagents as Context Firewalls
chapters.tease: A subagent's real gift is a clean context: it absorbs the noisy work and hands back a tidy note.

chapters.title: The Cost of More Agents
chapters.tease: Every agent you add charges in tokens, latency, failure surface and debuggability. Count all four first.

chapters.title: Shape Follows Failure
chapters.tease: Choose an architecture by imagining how each option fails, and pick the failures you can live with.

chapters.title: Tools Are an Interface
chapters.tease: A tool is a user interface, and its user is a literal reader with no access to your wiki.

chapters.title: Name It Like You Mean It
chapters.tease: The model reads tool names and descriptions with total care and believes them. Write them to be obeyed.

chapters.title: Fewer, Fatter Tools
chapters.tease: Forty endpoints should not become forty tools. Design a few tools around tasks, not around the schema.

chapters.title: Schemas That Refuse Nonsense
chapters.tease: Catch bad arguments at the border: a strict schema, then semantic checks in code, then execute.

chapters.title: Errors the Model Can Read
chapters.tease: Error messages are instructions in disguise. Say what happened, why, and what to do next.

chapters.title: Return What Matters
chapters.tease: Tool output spends the model's attention. Return a short briefing note, not a database dump.

chapters.title: Idempotent by Design
chapters.tease: Every write will be attempted twice one day. Design so the second attempt is a harmless no-op.

chapters.title: Read Tools and Write Tools
chapters.tease: Read tools observe the world; write tools change it. Give each class its own rules, and price writes higher.

chapters.title: Standard Plugs
chapters.tease: A standard protocol lets many agents reuse tool servers. It standardises the socket, not the quality.

chapters.title: Test Your Tools Like an API
chapters.tease: The model uses whatever your tool does, bugs included, with total sincerity. Test tools like any API.

chapters.title: Context Is a Budget
chapters.tease: More context does not make a better agent. Spend the window like a budget, on the decision at hand.

chapters.title: The System Prompt Is a Job Description
chapters.tease: Write the system prompt as a job description for a capable new hire, at the right altitude.

chapters.title: Just in Time Beats Just in Case
chapters.tease: Do not preload everything just in case. Give the agent an index and tools to fetch what it needs.

chapters.title: Retrieval Is a Tool
chapters.tease: Retrieval works best as a tool the model calls, refines and calls again, not a fixed step before it runs.

chapters.title: Compaction Without Amnesia
chapters.tease: Compaction lets agents run for hours, if the summary keeps the specifics: goal, decisions, dead ends, ids.

chapters.title: Notes to Self
chapters.tease: Keep notes outside the context window. When it is compacted or the run crashes, the notes remain.

chapters.title: Memory Across Sessions
chapters.tease: Long-term memory makes agents useful, or creepy, wrong and insecure. Design what to keep and how to forget.

chapters.title: Stale Context Is Wrong Context
chapters.tease: Facts captured last month go stale silently. Date and source every piece of context, and check live.

chapters.title: Caching the Stable Prefix
chapters.tease: Prompt caching reuses the stable start of a prompt. Put stable content first and variable content last.

chapters.title: Context Engineering
chapters.tease: Context engineering assembles exactly the right tokens for each step, by code, within a budget.

chapters.title: Agents Are Long-Running Processes
chapters.tease: An agent that runs for ten minutes is not a web request. It is a job, with states, an id and an owner.

chapters.title: Checkpoint Everything
chapters.tease: Save the agent's state after every step, so a crashed run resumes at step fourteen, not step one.

chapters.title: Durable Execution
chapters.tease: Write the loop as ordinary code; a durable engine records every call and replays results after a crash.

chapters.title: Retries With Manners
chapters.tease: Retry transient failures politely, in one layer only, and never retry errors that will not change.

chapters.title: Timeouts at Every Layer
chapters.tease: Every call, step and run needs a deadline that nests, and every timeout needs a defined outcome.

chapters.title: Exactly Once Is a Myth
chapters.tease: Exactly once is impossible. At-least-once delivery plus idempotent processing makes twice look like once.

chapters.title: Loops That Never End
chapters.tease: Runaway loops are the most expensive bug. Cap every run, detect repeats, and fix the causes.

chapters.title: Graceful Degradation
chapters.tease: When a dependency fails, do less and say so. Never carry on as if nothing happened.

chapters.title: Queues and Backpressure
chapters.tease: A queue absorbs bursts; backpressure tells it when to stop growing; limits protect the dependencies.

chapters.title: Compensation and Undo
chapters.tease: Most agent actions cannot be rolled back. Pair each write with a compensation; commit irreversible steps last.

chapters.title: Least Privilege, Most Sleep
chapters.tease: Give the agent only the access its task needs, because that bounds the damage, whatever goes wrong.

chapters.title: Guardrails Live Outside the Prompt
chapters.tease: A rule in the prompt changes a probability. A check in code holds whatever the model decides.

chapters.title: Input and Output Filters
chapters.tease: Screen what comes in before the agent sees it, and what goes out before anyone else does.

chapters.title: Approval Gates
chapters.tease: For consequential actions, the harness suspends the run, a human signs, and exactly that action executes.

chapters.title: Designing the Approval Screen
chapters.tease: An approval is only as good as what the approver sees. Show what the action does, not its name.

chapters.title: Rubber Stamp Fatigue
chapters.tease: Ask humans to approve too much and they learn to approve everything. Send fewer, better-chosen requests.

chapters.title: Escalation Paths
chapters.tease: Escalation is a tool, a queue and an owner, not a vague instruction to escalate if unsure.

chapters.title: Spend Limits and Rate Limits
chapters.tease: Hard caps at four levels, enforced by the harness, stop one bad run from becoming a bill or a flood.

chapters.title: Policy as Code
chapters.tease: Put every rule about what the agent may do in one versioned file, checked by software before every call.

chapters.title: Humans Are Part of the System
chapters.tease: Approvers, reviewers and operators are parts of the system. Design their roles as carefully as the code.

chapters.title: Everything Is Untrusted Input
chapters.tease: To a model, any text can read as an instruction, so everything you did not write is untrusted input.

chapters.title: Prompt Injection, Plainly
chapters.tease: Indirect injection arrives in content the agent reads for someone else. Design so success does not matter.

chapters.title: The Lethal Trifecta
chapters.tease: Private data, untrusted content and a way out, all in one agent: remove any one and the attack fails.

chapters.title: Secrets Stay Out of Context
chapters.tease: Credentials live in the harness, never in the model's window. A model cannot leak what it never saw.

chapters.title: Scoped Credentials
chapters.tease: A credential should be a key to one room, issued for one visit: narrow capability, one subject, short life.

chapters.title: Sandboxes and Blast Radius
chapters.tease: Running code is the most powerful capability. Contain it so whatever happens inside cannot reach what matters.

chapters.title: Acting on Behalf of Whom
chapters.tease: An agent's authority should never exceed that of whoever it is working for. Carry their identity through.

chapters.title: Supply Chain for Tools
chapters.tease: Every tool server you install writes part of your prompt. Review it, pin it, isolate it and watch it.

chapters.title: Red Team Your Own Agent
chapters.tease: Find your agent's weaknesses by attacking it, deliberately and regularly, before a stranger does.

chapters.title: Security Is a Property of the Design
chapters.tease: You cannot prompt a model into being secure. You can design a system where a fooled model does little harm.

chapters.title: Every Token Has an Owner
chapters.tease: Tag every model call with its run, feature, tenant and versions, and any spending question becomes a query.

chapters.title: Budgets per Run
chapters.tease: Per-run budgets turn the open-ended cost tail into a known ceiling, set just above the 99th percentile.

chapters.title: Latency Is a Feature
chapters.tease: Latency decides whether people use the agent at all. Measure where the seconds go, then cut the biggest.

chapters.title: Right-Size the Model
chapters.tease: Use the largest model where it changes the answer, and the smallest one everywhere else.

chapters.title: Streaming and Progress
chapters.tease: A visible trail of what the agent is doing beats a spinner: faster-feeling, more trusted, and stoppable.

chapters.title: Traces Not Logs
chapters.tease: An agent run is a tree of spans, not a list of log lines. Trace it so you can see why, not just what.

chapters.title: What to Record
chapters.tease: Record enough to explain any decision, and keep it no longer than you need to.

chapters.title: Dashboards That Answer Questions
chapters.tease: Start from the four questions people ask, and show exactly the numbers that answer them.

chapters.title: Reading a Trace
chapters.tease: Read a bad run like a story: find the first wrong turn, because everything after it is consequence.

chapters.title: Observability Closes the Loop
chapters.tease: Production traces and feedback are raw material: feed them into evals and the agent improves every week.

chapters.title: Evals Are Your Spec
chapters.tease: An evaluation set is your specification in executable form: the cases you care about and how to judge them.

chapters.title: Building the First Eval Set
chapters.tease: Start with twenty real cases you understand completely, each with a specific expected outcome, and grow.

chapters.title: Grading Outcomes Not Paths
chapters.tease: Grade whether the end state is right, not whether the agent took your favourite route there.

chapters.title: Models as Graders
chapters.tease: A model grader is a measuring instrument: give it a specific rubric, check it against humans, know its biases.

chapters.title: Regression Suites
chapters.tease: Turn every fixed failure into a permanent test, run several times, so what was fixed stays fixed.

chapters.title: Pass Rates and Variance
chapters.tease: One run is an anecdote. Run each case several times and think in pass rates, ranges and consistency.

chapters.title: Shadow Mode
chapters.tease: Let the agent handle real traffic in parallel, recording not acting, and compare it with what people did.

chapters.title: Canaries and Gradual Rollout
chapters.tease: Ship to a few, watch closely, then ship to more. Rollout in stages turns one gamble into small bets.

chapters.title: Versioning Everything
chapters.tease: Version every component that shapes behaviour, bundle them into one numbered release, record it per run.

chapters.title: Changing the Model Underneath
chapters.tease: Changing the model is not a configuration tweak. It is a migration, and it deserves the care of one.

chapters.title: On Call for an Agent
chapters.tease: On call for an agent means alerting on quiet wrongness as well as errors, with a runbook strangers can use.

chapters.title: The Kill Switch
chapters.tease: Every agent needs a boring red button: four sizes, checked before every step, usable by anyone on call.

chapters.title: Incident Response for Agents
chapters.tease: Detect, contain, investigate, remediate, review. For agents, contain first: they do not pause while you think.

chapters.title: The Blameless Postmortem
chapters.tease: Do not stop at blaming the model or a person. Ask why the system let the error through, and fix that.

chapters.title: Drift Happens
chapters.tease: Agents rarely fail in a day. They drift a point a fortnight, and no alert fires. Look for slopes, not spikes.

chapters.title: Governance Without Theatre
chapters.tease: Govern with an inventory, named owners and review scaled to risk: make the right thing easy, not paperwork.

chapters.title: Audit Trails
chapters.tease: An audit trail lets you say exactly what the agent did, for whom, under what authority, and with what result.

chapters.title: Explaining the Agent to the Business
chapters.tease: Promise the error rate and the safety net, never perfection, and say it in the business's own terms.

chapters.title: Boring Is the Goal
chapters.tease: A mature agent is dull from the outside: quiet, predictable, trusted. That dullness is the ambition, achieved.

chapters.title: Reliability Is Designed, Not Prompted
chapters.tease: A prompt makes good behaviour likelier. Only design makes bad outcomes bounded, visible and recoverable.
